newsitem.title: UK: Russian ambassador pleads for NATO treaty.
newsitem.headline: Russian ambassador pleads for NATO treaty.

text.p: Russia's ambassador to Britain on Wednesday pleaded for a legally-binding treaty between Moscow and NATO which he said would allay Russian fears over the expansion of the alliance.

Moscow, which sees NATO's planned expansion to incorporate the former Soviet states of eastern Europe as a threat and a political embarrassment, has called for a treaty setting out its relations with NATO. The West wants to avoid a treaty needing parliamentary approval.
But ambassador Anatoly Adamishin said such a treaty could be built up gradually.
"Russia does not seek to have its voice given equal weight on all questions immediately," said Adamishin, writing in Thursday's The European newspaper.

"On those matters that touch its vital national interests, Russia's voice should be no less weighty than that of NATO," Adamishin said. "The principle of equality should be paramount from the very beginning."
U.S. Secretary or State Madeleine Albright said after meeting Russian President Boris Yeltsin last week that she had made "important progress" on the issue but that much more work was needed.
Yeltsin has said he has agreed to look for a compromise on NATO expansion when he meets U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki in March.
But Russian opposition to the proposed enlargement of NATO remains widespread and hostile.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov earlier this week warned that the army was heading for financial ruin and that the West might therefore try to place Russia's nuclear arsenal under United Nations control.
Adamishin said he, too, believed NATO enlargement was a mistake which would lead to increased military expenditure and would set back reconciliation between Russia and the West.
"For how long are we to go on being generals preparing for a past war," he asked.
Would it not be possible to transform the idea of NATO's enlargement so that it could help create a genuinely collective security system, Adamishin wondered.
"If NATO truly transformed itself in this way it would lead to its changing its name, which has too many odious associations in Russia.
"After all we are not the USSR any more," he said.
